cards.lead: Wootz crucible steel in South India
cards.note: The earliest dated site evidence is Kodumanal, dated to about the 2nd century BC, not c. 300 BCE. The steel-bearing crucibles from Mel-Siruvalur are not dated in the source read. Whether South Indian crucible steel was independent of Central Asian practice is not settled by the sources read.
cards.name: Wootz crucible steel, South India
cards.summary: Making uniform high-carbon steel in sealed crucibles in South India, the material behind the wootz tradition.
cards.description: Crucible fragments from the surface collection at Mel-Siruvalur in Tamil Nadu contained iron prills of uniform high-carbon steel, about 1 to 1.5 percent carbon. Crucible fragments from the excavated megalithic site of Kodumanal, near Karur, are dated to about the 2nd century BC and have a fabric similar to those from Mel-Siruvalur. The sources read do not date the steel production at Mel-Siruvalur.
cards.origin_note: The sources read do not establish whether South Indian crucible steel was independent of the Central Asian crucible steel at Merv.

impact.note: Lead scores kept; the sources read give no reason to change them.

cards.note: A Banco de la República chronology of Colombian metallurgy (Boletín del Museo del Oro) says the early Sinú dates for cast items were still to be confirmed, and it gives no secure earliest date for lost-wax casting. Searches did not find a securely dated earliest lost-wax casting in Colombia or a dated spread into Panama, Costa Rica or Mexico. The curator's date of c. 500 BCE is not supported by the sources read.

The dated evidence gives the objects as the ninth to twelfth centuries AD, not the ninth to tenth. The sources read say the metal probably came from the nearby Abakaliki source, but do not settle whether the casting technique was invented locally or introduced.
cards.name: Lost-wax bronze casting, Igbo-Ukwu
cards.summary: Local lost-wax casting in bronze and leaded bronze at Igbo-Ukwu in eastern Nigeria, using metal from the nearby Abakaliki source.
cards.description: Earlier studies concluded that most of the Igbo-Ukwu copper-alloy objects were predominantly lost-wax castings of bronze or leaded bronze, dated to approximately the ninth to twelfth centuries AD. The 2022 metallographic study found that some components were hammered instead, and that trace elements suggest most of the metal came from the nearby Abakaliki source.
cards.origin_note: The 2022 study reports local Abakaliki metal but does not settle whether the casting technique was invented locally or came from outside.

impact.note: Lead scores kept; the sources read give no reason to change them.

cards.lead: Patio-process silver amalgamation in New Spain
cards.note: The Spanish study read dates Medina's first use of the mercury method at the Purísima Grande mine in Pachuca to 1555, and gives 1553 or 1554 for his arrival in Mexico. The 1554 date in the lead is therefore not confirmed by this source.
cards.name: Patio-process silver amalgamation, Pachuca
cards.summary: Cold mercury amalgamation of silver ore on open patios at Pachuca, which made low-grade silver ore worth working in New Spain.
cards.description: Bartolomé de Medina put his mercury amalgamation method into practice at the Purísima Grande mine in Pachuca in 1555, according to a Spanish study of the period. Crushed ore was mixed with salt and water, then with mercury and copper sulphate, and trodden by horses on a paved patio. The study describes the method as used on an industrial scale from the mid-16th century in Mexico.
cards.origin_note: The study says amalgamation was known from very early times, and that Medina knew the method only in theory, from talks with a German in Spain, before he perfected it in Mexico. The record is therefore not clearly first or independent.

impact.note: Lead scores kept; the sources read give no reason to change them.

cards.why: Medina wanted to extract silver without costly smelting and refining, and came to New Spain to test the idea.

cards.note: The source read dates Keller's wood-grinding machine to 1843 and his German patent (with Voelter) to August 1845, not 1843 to 1846. Matthias Koops produced paper from wood pulp in England in 1801, so Keller is first for the groundwood process rather than for wood-pulp paper. Keller and Fenerty are said to have independently announced similar processes in 1844.
cards.name: Groundwood pulp paper, Saxony
cards.summary: Friedrich Gottlob Keller's wood-grinding machine of 1843 produced groundwood pulp suitable for papermaking, in place of rags.
cards.description: In 1843 Friedrich Gottlob Keller invented a wood-grinding machine that produced groundwood pulp suitable for papermaking. A German patent of August 1845 went to Keller and Heinrich Voelter, and the process was then commercialised by Voelter and Johann Matthäus Voith. Charles Fenerty announced a similar process with spruce-wood paper in Halifax, Nova Scotia, in October 1844.
cards.origin_note: One source says Keller and Fenerty both appear to have independently announced similar processes in 1844, and that Matthias Koops had produced paper from wood pulp in England as early as 1801.

impact.note: Lead scores kept; the sources read give no reason to change them.

cards.why: The systematic search for substitute raw materials for paper in Europe had proved difficult, so a practical wood-based pulp was needed.

cards.name: Phenol-formaldehyde resin (Bakelite), Yonkers
cards.summary: Leo Baekeland's heat-set phenol-formaldehyde resin, developed in Yonkers by 1907, was the first totally synthetic plastic and was introduced in 1909.
cards.description: Leo Hendrik Baekeland developed a totally synthetic thermosetting plastic in Yonkers, New York, by controlling phenol and formaldehyde reactions under heat and pressure in a closed reactor. In 1907 he opened the reactor to find a clear solid that was heat resistant, nonconducting and machinable. Bakelite was introduced to the scientific community in 1909 and quickly found industrial uses, particularly in parts for the automobile sector.
cards.origin_note: The source calls Baekeland the first person to produce a completely artificial plastic; earlier celluloid and casein plastics were derivatives of natural products.

impact.note: Lead scores kept; the sources read give no reason to change them.

cards.why: Baekeland sought a cheap substitute for shellac, which had a wide market; when a solvent for the resin failed, he developed an insoluble resin instead.

events.statement: Baekeland's experiments in Yonkers produced a clear solid that was heat resistant, nonconducting and machinable.
events.quote: In 1907, his meticulous experiments paid off when he opened the reactor to find that he had created a clear solid that was heat resistant, nonconducting, and machinable.
